words.definition: To bring someone to a calmer state by yielding to their wishes or demands.
words.example: To appease the wailing toddler, she quietly handed over the last cookie.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'a peace' — you make a peace with someone to appease them.

words.definition: To reduce another person's anger or distress and make them feel better.
words.example: A sincere apology and a free dessert helped mollify the furious diner.
words.mnemonic: 'Molli-' sounds like 'mellow' — you make an angry person mellow.

words.definition: To calm an angry or dissatisfied person, usually by doing something that pleases them.
words.example: The airline offered hotel vouchers to placate passengers stranded overnight.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'plac-' as in 'placid' (calm) — you make someone placid again.

words.definition: To bring peace to someone or something, ending anger, unrest, or fighting.
words.example: The nanny gently rocked the infant to pacify her before bedtime.
words.mnemonic: Think 'Pacific Ocean' (peaceful) and a baby's 'pacifier' — both calm things down.

words.definition: To win over goodwill or end a dispute by acting in a friendly, agreeable way.
words.example: The mediator worked patiently to conciliate the two feuding departments.
words.mnemonic: 'Concili-' as in 'council' and 'reconcile' — bring both sides to a council to make peace.

words.definition: To gain the favor of a powerful or angry being, often through an offering.
words.example: The villagers left fruit at the shrine to propitiate the mountain spirits.
words.mnemonic: 'Pro-piti-ate' — offer up 'a pie' (or your pity) to a god to win its favor.

words.definition: To make an unpleasant feeling less intense, or to satisfy a craving.
words.example: A glass of cold water did little to assuage her thirst in the desert heat.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'a-swage' → 'a massage' — a good massage eases your aches.

words.definition: To make something harmful, painful, or severe less serious.
words.example: Planting shade trees along the avenue helped mitigate the summer heat.
words.mnemonic: 'Miti-gate' — a gate that holds back the 'mighty' danger, weakening its force.

words.definition: To make a bad or unsatisfactory situation better.
words.example: The new medication ameliorated his chronic back pain within a few days.
words.mnemonic: Hidden Latin root 'melior' means 'better' — think 'a-MELIOR-ate' = to make better.

words.definition: To make pain or a problem easier to bear or less serious.
words.example: She took an aspirin to alleviate her pounding headache before the meeting.
words.mnemonic: 'A-LEVI-ate' — from 'levis' (light); you lift and lighten the burden.

words.definition: To bring under control by force, or to make quieter and less intense.
words.example: It took four officers to subdue the struggling, panicked suspect.
words.mnemonic: 'Sub-due' — 'sub' means under; you force something down and under your control.

words.definition: To defeat an enemy or opponent completely in a battle or contest.
words.example: The young knight vowed to vanquish the dragon terrorizing the realm.
words.mnemonic: 'Van-quish' — make your enemy 'vanish' once you've quished them for good.

words.definition: To prevent someone from accomplishing a plan or goal.
words.example: Alert guards thwarted the burglars before they ever reached the vault.
words.mnemonic: 'Thwart' sounds like a 'thwack' plus a 'wart' — an obstacle that smacks a plan flat.

words.definition: To stop a plan or attempt from succeeding.
words.example: A stubbornly locked window foiled the intruder's attempt to break in.
words.mnemonic: Picture a fencer's 'foil' sword parrying a thrust — it blocks the attack cold.

words.definition: To block or hinder someone's progress toward a goal.
words.example: A single missing signature was enough to stymie the entire merger for months.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like "sty + me" — imagine a muddy pig sty blocking your path, trapping me so I can't move forward.

words.definition: To slow down an action or make it more difficult.
words.example: Thick fog impeded the rescuers as they climbed toward the stranded hikers.
words.mnemonic: im-PEDE — from 'ped' (foot, as in pedal); imagine your foot caught, slowing every step.

words.definition: To block a path or get in the way of something.
words.example: A fallen oak obstructed the road, forcing every car to turn around.
words.mnemonic: ob-STRUCT — a 'structure' planted squarely in your way.

words.definition: Eager to fight or behaving in a hostile, aggressive way.
words.example: After his third drink, the belligerent customer began shouting at the waiter.
words.mnemonic: 'belli-' is Latin for war (as in antebellum); this person is spoiling for war.

words.definition: Naturally quick to argue or start a fight.
words.example: The pugnacious little terrier squared up to dogs three times its size.
words.mnemonic: PUG-nacious — picture a pug throwing punches (Latin 'pugnus,' fist).

words.definition: Ready and eager to argue or fight.
words.example: Her combative tone turned a simple question into a heated dispute.
words.mnemonic: COMBAT-ive — full of combat, always braced for a scrap.

words.definition: To make someone feel hostile or angry toward you.
words.example: He antagonized his neighbors by blasting music at three in the morning.
words.mnemonic: Think of the 'antagonist' — the villain who stirs up the hero's fury.

words.definition: To deliberately cause a strong or angry reaction in someone.
words.example: The reporter's pointed questions were clearly meant to provoke the senator.
words.mnemonic: pro-VOKE — from 'vocare' (to call); you call a reaction forth.

words.definition: To urge or stir people into taking violent or unlawful action.
words.example: The pamphlet was banned for trying to incite workers to storm the factory gates.
words.mnemonic: in-CITE — like lighting a fire inside a crowd (Latin 'citare,' to rouse).

words.definition: To secretly stir up trouble, rebellion, or bad feeling.
words.example: Rival agents worked quietly to foment unrest among the border villages.
words.mnemonic: FO-ment sounds like 'ferment' — you let resentment ferment and bubble over.

words.definition: To bring about or set in motion, especially trouble.
words.example: Investigators found that a single employee had instigated the whole scheme.
words.mnemonic: in-STIG-ate — picture poking with a 'stick' to get things moving.

words.definition: To keep prodding someone until they react or act.
words.example: His teammates goaded him into jumping off the highest rock into the lake.
words.mnemonic: A 'goad' is a pointed stick for driving cattle — you poke to force movement.

words.definition: To cause lasting irritation, resentment, or bitterness in someone.
words.example: The unfair demotion still rankled years after she had left the company.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'ankle' — imagine a sore ankle that keeps festering and won't heal.

words.definition: To involve someone deeply in a conflict or difficult situation.
words.example: A careless email embroiled the manager in a lawsuit that dragged on for years.
words.mnemonic: em-BROIL — to cook someone inside a hot, messy 'broil' of trouble.

words.definition: Disagreement or lack of harmony between people.
words.example: Years of discord between the two founders finally split the company in half.
words.mnemonic: dis- (apart) + 'cord' (heart, from 'cor') — hearts pulled apart; the opposite of concord.

words.definition: Bitter conflict or angry disagreement between people or groups.
words.example: Years of political strife left the small nation exhausted and its citizens longing for calm.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'strive' — people who strive against each other produce constant fighting.

words.definition: Deep hatred or ill will felt toward an opponent.
words.example: The enmity between the two families had simmered for generations, poisoning every chance meeting.
words.mnemonic: Enmity hides the word 'enemy' — it's the feeling you hold toward an enemy.

words.definition: A strong feeling of dislike or hatred, often openly shown.
words.example: You could sense the animosity in her clipped replies whenever his name came up.
words.mnemonic: 'Anim-' (spirit) + sounds like 'atrocity' — a spirit turned atrocious toward someone.

words.definition: A deep, instinctive feeling of dislike or aversion.
words.example: She felt an immediate antipathy toward the smug new manager, though she couldn't explain why.
words.mnemonic: 'Anti-' (against) + '-pathy' (feeling) — a feeling set against someone.

words.definition: A long, bitter quarrel between two people, families, or groups.
words.example: The bakery and the deli next door had been locked in a feud over parking for a decade.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'stewed' — a grudge that stays stewing between families for years.

words.definition: A split into opposing factions, often within a church or organization.
words.example: A bitter schism divided the congregation after the vote on the new hymnal.
words.mnemonic: Starts like 'scissors' — a schism cuts a group cleanly into two parts.

words.definition: A serious break in friendly relations between people or groups.
words.example: A careless comment at dinner opened a rift between the brothers that lasted years.
words.mnemonic: A rift is a crack in the earth — picture a widening crack splitting two friends apart.

words.definition: A heated fight, contest, or noisy dispute.
words.example: The rookie senator jumped straight into the fray, trading barbs during his first debate.
words.mnemonic: Fray sounds like 'afraid' — but the brave dive into the fray, the noisy fight.

words.definition: A brief, minor fight between small groups, often part of a larger conflict.
words.example: A skirmish broke out at the border before the main armies had even arrived.
words.mnemonic: Skirmish sounds like 'skirt + rush' — soldiers rushing at the skirts (edges) of a battle.

words.definition: A noisy, heated argument or dispute.
words.example: The altercation over the parking space escalated until a bystander called security.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'alter' — an altercation is two people loudly trying to alter each other's view.

words.definition: A noisy, disorderly disturbance or brawl involving several people.
words.example: Police were called when a fracas erupted among fans outside the stadium gates.
words.mnemonic: Fracas blends 'fracture' + 'ruckus' — a ruckus that fractures the peace.

words.definition: A confused, chaotic fight involving a crowd of people.
words.example: In the melee after the concert, she lost both her shoes and her phone.
words.mnemonic: Melee sounds like 'mail-ay' — imagine a jumbled pile of mail, all chaos and confusion.

words.definition: A rough, noisy fight involving several people, usually with fists.
words.example: A bar brawl spilled onto the sidewalk, chairs flying and glasses shattering.
words.mnemonic: Brawl rhymes with 'bawl' and 'sprawl' — bodies sprawl as fighters bawl.

words.definition: A long, complicated argument, often over small details.
words.example: After a three-hour wrangle over the budget, the committee still hadn't agreed on anything.
words.mnemonic: Wrangle blends 'wrestle' + 'tangle' — you wrestle and get tangled in a dispute.

words.definition: A petty, noisy quarrel over something unimportant.
words.example: The children fell into a squabble over who got the last slice of cake.
words.mnemonic: Squabble sounds like 'squawk' — picture two birds squawking over a single crumb.

words.definition: To argue or box lightly as practice, without intending real harm.
words.example: The two candidates sparred over tax policy throughout the televised debate.
words.mnemonic: Picture a boxing SPARring partner throwing playful practice punches — nobody's really trying to hurt anyone.

words.definition: To compete eagerly with others in order to win or achieve something.
words.example: The two startups vie for the same customers, each slashing prices to win them.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like the start of "rivalry" (ri-VAL) — to vie is to act like a rival.

words.definition: An ongoing competition or hostility between people or groups chasing the same goal.
words.example: The rivalry between the two schools turned every match into a sellout.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like "river-y" — two enemies on opposite RIVER banks, forever refusing to cross.

words.definition: A temporary agreement between enemies to stop fighting for a while.
words.example: The squabbling children called a truce and split the last cookie.
words.mnemonic: "Truce" squishes TRUe + peaCE — a brief, genuine pause in the fighting.

words.definition: A formal agreement between warring sides to end active fighting.
words.example: The armistice of 1918 finally silenced the guns on the Western Front.
words.mnemonic: ARMistice — the signal to lay down your ARMS (weapons) and stop the war.

words.definition: A formal agreement, or a state of mutual understanding between parties.
words.example: After months of talks, the two nations signed a peace accord.
words.mnemonic: Say it "a chord" — like musical notes in a chord that blend together in agreement.

words.definition: A state of peaceful agreement and friendly relations among people.
words.example: The neighboring villages lived in concord, freely sharing water and grazing land.
words.mnemonic: CON (with) + CORD — hearts tied together by a single CORD, pulling the same way.

words.definition: A friendly and peaceful relationship between people or nations.
words.example: Decades of amity between the two countries made the shared border almost invisible.
words.mnemonic: Hear the French "ami" (friend) inside it — amity is pure friendSHIP.

words.definition: A renewal of warm relations between people or countries after conflict.
words.example: The historic handshake signaled a rapprochement after years of cold silence.
words.mnemonic: Spot "approach" buried inside — two former enemies APPROACH each other again to make peace.

words.definition: To restore friendship after a quarrel, or make two things agree.
words.example: After the bitter argument, the sisters reconciled over a long, tearful phone call.
words.mnemonic: RE-council — call both sides back to the COUNCIL table to settle their differences.

words.definition: A peaceful state of agreement, or a pleasing combination of musical notes.
words.example: The four roommates lived in perfect harmony, never once fighting over chores.
words.mnemonic: No one gets HARMed when a household lives in harmony — like notes blending sweetly.

words.definition: To surrender or give in completely after putting up resistance.
words.example: Outnumbered and exhausted, the garrison finally capitulated to the besieging army.
words.mnemonic: The CAPITAL city falls, so the leader raises the white flag — CAPITULate means give up.

words.definition: To accept or agree to something reluctantly, without protesting.
words.example: She disliked the plan, but she acquiesced to keep the peace at dinner.
words.mnemonic: Hear "quiet" in the middle (quiesce) — you go QUIET and simply let it happen.

words.definition: To become less harsh or stubborn and finally give in.
words.example: Her father refused at first, but relented when she promised to be home by ten.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like "lenient" — to relent is to turn LENIENT and bend a little.

words.definition: To do something good to make up for having done something bad.
words.example: He spent years volunteering at the shelter to atone for the harm his lies had caused.
words.mnemonic: AT + ONE: you make things right so you and the person you wronged are 'at one' again.

words.definition: To make up for guilt or sin through suffering or good deeds.
words.example: The knight undertook a dangerous pilgrimage to expiate the cruelty of his younger years.
words.mnemonic: EX-PIE-ate: eat a slice of humble PIE to cancel out your sin.

words.definition: The setting right of a wrong, or payment for damage or injustice.
words.example: The laid-off workers marched to demand redress for months of unpaid wages.
words.mnemonic: RE-DRESS: you 'dress' a wound a second time to fix the harm.

words.definition: Compensation given for a wrong or injury, often after a war.
words.example: The defeated nation was forced to pay reparations to the countries it had invaded.
words.mnemonic: REPARATION hides 'repair' — money paid to REPAIR the damage done.

words.definition: The return of something lost or stolen to its rightful owner.
words.example: The court ordered the burglar to make restitution to every family he had robbed.
words.mnemonic: RE-STITUTION ≈ 're-institute': put everything back the way it was.

words.definition: To officially declare someone free from blame or guilt.
words.example: After she confessed everything, the priest absolved her and sent her home in peace.
words.mnemonic: AB-SOLVE: to 'solve away' the guilt, dissolving all blame.

words.definition: To clear someone of a charge or accusation of wrongdoing.
words.example: New DNA evidence exonerated the man after he had spent twenty years in prison.
words.mnemonic: EX (out) + ONUS (burden): the burden of blame is lifted right off you.

words.definition: To declare in a court that a person is not guilty.
words.example: The jury acquitted her because the prosecution never produced any real evidence.
words.mnemonic: AC-QUIT: the court lets you 'quit' the charges and walk free.

words.definition: To officially forgive someone and cancel their punishment for a crime.
words.example: The governor pardoned the prisoner just hours before the scheduled execution.
words.mnemonic: PAR-DON: a powerful 'don' grants forgiveness from on high.

words.definition: Mercy shown by a person who has the power to punish.
words.example: The judge showed clemency, handing the young offender community service instead of jail.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'clement' weather — mild and gentle, never harsh.

words.definition: To accept or overlook wrong behavior without objecting to it.
words.example: The coach refused to condone cheating, even when it might have won the championship.
words.mnemonic: CON-DONE: treat the wrong as 'done and gone' — just let it slide.

words.definition: To help two opposing sides reach an agreement by acting between them.
words.example: A neutral counselor was brought in to mediate between the divorcing couple.
words.mnemonic: MEDI = 'middle': you stand in the middle to settle the fight.

words.definition: To settle a dispute by making a binding decision as a neutral judge.
words.example: Both companies agreed to let an outside expert arbitrate their contract disagreement.
words.mnemonic: Think 'arbiter' — the appointed judge whose ruling everyone must accept.

words.definition: To discuss something in order to reach an agreement or deal.
words.example: The union spent weeks trying to negotiate a fair pay raise with management.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'negotium' (business) — you're doing business to hammer out a deal.

words.definition: A discussion between enemies to settle a dispute or agree on terms.
words.example: Under a white flag, the two generals met to parley before the final battle.
words.mnemonic: From French 'parler' (to speak): foes speak instead of fight.

words.definition: A person who arranges deals or transactions between two other parties for a fee.
words.example: The couple hired a broker to help them find and buy their first home.
words.mnemonic: Read it as 'broke-er': the middleman who breaks a big deal down into an agreement both sides can accept.

words.definition: To leave quickly and secretly, often to avoid arrest or while carrying stolen goods.
words.example: The treasurer absconded with the company funds and was never seen again.
words.mnemonic: ABSCOND = 'absent' + 'con(vict)': the con makes himself absent, slipping away with the loot.

words.definition: Present but hidden or not yet active or developed.
words.example: Her latent talent for singing surfaced only when a friend handed her a microphone.
words.mnemonic: LATENT sounds like 'lay-tent': it lies quietly in a tent, waiting to emerge.

words.definition: Spreading widely through every part of something.
words.example: A pervasive smell of smoke filled every room in the house.
words.mnemonic: PER-VADE (Latin vadere, 'to go'): it goes through and through everything.

words.definition: Not likely to cause harm or offense; completely safe.
words.example: What seemed an innocuous comment somehow started a huge argument at dinner.
words.mnemonic: Shares 'inno-' with 'innocent': an innocent thing does no harm.

words.definition: Harmful or poisonous to living things.
words.example: Noxious fumes from the factory forced nearby residents to evacuate.
words.mnemonic: Think 'obnoxious' plus 'toxic' (Latin noxa, 'harm'): a smell so toxic it harms you.

words.definition: Overused and therefore lacking originality or freshness.
words.example: His apology felt trite, full of the same empty phrases everyone uses.
words.mnemonic: TRITE sounds like 'tried': an idea tried so many times it's worn thin.

words.definition: Acting with care and good judgment about the future.
words.example: It was prudent of them to save money before quitting their jobs.
words.mnemonic: PRUDENT starts like 'prude': a prude is careful and cautious — so is a prudent planner.

words.definition: Able to accurately judge situations and turn them to advantage.
words.example: An astute investor, she sold her shares just before the market crashed.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'a stew': an astute chef tastes the stew and instantly knows exactly what it needs.

words.definition: Having a keen ability to notice and understand things clearly.
words.example: The perspicacious detective spotted the one detail everyone else had missed.
words.mnemonic: Hidden 'spic' (Latin specere, 'to see', as in inspect/spectacle): someone who sees right through things.

words.definition: Showing good judgment and the ability to notice fine distinctions.
words.example: A discerning wine taster can identify the vineyard from a single sip.
words.mnemonic: Root 'cern' means 'to sift/separate': a mind that sifts apart the finest differences.

words.definition: Slow to understand; annoyingly lacking in quick perception.
words.example: He was so obtuse that he missed every hint she dropped about the surprise party.
words.mnemonic: An obtuse angle is wide and blunt; an obtuse mind is just as blunt and dull.
